also: anywhere (after not, if, or in a question)

evidence: Ter. Ad. 3.4.7: utinam hīc prope adesset alicubi (Lewis & Short)
Atticus in Cic. Att. 9.10: sī salvus sit Pompejus et cōnstiterit alicubi (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Some one place, not named; Lewis & Short, after Priscian: alicubi points to some place, usquam to any place at all.

evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: cum aliquō exībimus
terms.comment: Of going: aliquō exīre, to go off somewhere.
Also “from somebody”: alicunde sūmere, to borrow from someone (Ter. Ph. 2.1.70, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Att. 16.13b.1: malō esse in Tusculānō aut uspiam in suburbānō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare but classical; mostly in statements (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: anywhere (after a negative, in questions and conditions)
evidence: Liv. 21.22.6: neque usquam ā sē dēflecteret oculōs
Cic. Flac. 50: cui nūllus esset usquam cōnsistendī locus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The “anywhere” of negative sentences, as quisquam is the “anyone” (see someone); “nowhere” is nusquam (Lewis & Short).
“If … anywhere” in one word, as sī quis is “if anyone”.

phrases.english: if only he were somewhere near here

phrases.latin: quod ad Pompōniam, sī tibi vidētur, scrībās velim, cum aliquō exībimus eat nōbīscum puerumque ēdūcat.
phrases.english: as for Pomponia, please write to her, if you agree, that when we go off somewhere she should come with us and bring the boy.

phrases.latin: nē aut ille alserit, aut uspiam ceciderit, aut perfrēgerit aliquid
phrases.english: in case he has caught cold, or fallen somewhere, or broken something

phrases.latin: proinde sequerētur neque usquam ā sē dēflecteret oculōs
phrases.english: so he was to follow, and not turn his eyes from him anywhere
